2. ~(~I ≡ H) ≡ (~I and H) (not (~I) is equivalent to H)

Now, we can construct the truth table:

| I | H | ~I | ~I ≡ H | ~(~I ≡ H) | I ≡ ~H |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T | T | F | F | T | F |
| T | F | F | F | T | F |
| F | T | T | F | F | T |
| F | F | T | T | F | T |

From the truth table, we can see that:

- I ≡ ~H is a tautology (always true), and
- ~(~I ≡ H) is a contradiction (never true)

Since ~(~I ≡ H) is a contradiction and I ≡ ~H is a tautology, the two statements are logically equivalent. However, they are not consistent, because they cannot both be true at the same time.
